clue.text: Spirit shown by quartet in Dvorák intermezzo

indicators.note: a quartet is a set of four, so four consecutive letters are taken from inside the following words

parts.note: four letters running across the end of the composer's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A string quartet brings real spirit to an intermezzo by the Czech composer Dvorák.
explanation.walkthrough: The accent on the composer's name is ignored: the run is the last three letters of Dvorák plus the first of intermezzo.
explanation.definitionFit: Raki is an aniseed-flavoured liquor from Turkey and the Balkans, so a spirit in the drinks sense.

clue.text: Figures great-uncles lost heart performing

indicators.note: letters that are performing are acting out a new routine, so they are rearranged
losing its heart means the central letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: the relatives taken as written, eleven letters before the middle one goes

explanation.surface: Elderly relatives, having lost their nerve, still manage to put on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle (sixth) letter U of great-uncles is removed before the remaining ten letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Rectangles are geometric shapes, and figure is the standard word for a shape in geometry.

clue.text: Film of Ginger Rogers in pool with wartime detective

parts.note: a kitty is a shared pool of money
DCS Foyle is the detective of the British TV series Foyle's War, set in the Second World War

explanation.surface: Ginger Rogers stars in a movie alongside a pool and a wartime sleuth.
explanation.walkthrough: Foyle's War is a British TV drama about a police detective on the south coast during the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitty Foyle is the 1940 film for which Ginger Rogers won the Academy Award for Best Actress.

clue.text: Lyrics by quality poet

parts.note: the lyrics of a song are its words
worth is merit or quality

explanation.surface: Song lyrics written by a poet of real quality.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the English Romantic poet of the Lake District, author of the daffodils lines.

clue.text: Ear, perhaps, for a musical instrument

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a part of the body, of which the ear is one example
second meaning: the keyboard instrument with pipes found in churches

explanation.surface: Someone with a good ear might take up a musical instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The ear is a bodily organ, and the organ is also the large pipe instrument played in churches.

clue.text: Sell short sad standard

parts.note: feeling down is feeling sad
a grade is a level or standard

explanation.surface: A trader shorts a stock, a sad comment on its standard.
explanation.definitionFit: To sell someone short is to undervalue them, which is to belittle or demote them in estimation.

clue.text: Released with Cream hits, second song

indicators.note: released letters are set free from their order and allowed to fall into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: A band puts out a single alongside the hits of the rock group Cream.
explanation.walkthrough: Cream was the 1960s rock trio of Clapton, Bruce and Baker; here the band's name is just fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: White Christmas is the Irving Berlin song made famous by Bing Crosby, one of the best-selling singles ever.

clue.text: Peculiar piano seat

parts.note: rum is an old British word for odd or peculiar
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: An odd-looking stool for the pianist.
explanation.definitionFit: Rump is the buttocks, and seat is a common polite synonym for one's backside.

clue.text: Solo, last from Band Aid?

parts.note: Han Solo is the smuggler pilot in Star Wars

indicators.note: the last from a word means only its final letter is kept

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A solo spot, with the final word going to the 1984 charity group Band Aid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band Aid' looks like one name, the charity supergroup, but it splits: Band supplies a letter and Aid is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a hand is to help them, so hand works as a noun meaning assistance.

clue.text: Canned music producers?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: drunk, via the rhyming slang for a word meaning drunk

definitions.note: a plural noun defining a phrase that names two people, fair because the two composers together are the producers of the music
definitions.meaning: second meaning: two great nineteenth-century composers

explanation.surface: Who makes the recorded background music piped into shops?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canned music' reads as one phrase meaning muzak; split it. In Cockney rhyming slang Brahms and Liszt rhymes with 'pissed', British slang for drunk, as is canned.
explanation.definitionFit: Brahms and Liszt both composed music, and the pair's names together are British rhyming slang for being drunk.

clue.text: Retired teacher drinking at college dance

indicators.note: retiring is withdrawing or going back, so the letters run backwards
drinking takes something in, so one word swallows the next

parts.note: a guru is a spiritual teacher
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A retired teacher has a drink at the college ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The teacher holds AT, the college letter follows, and the whole string is then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Cut a rug is an old slang idiom meaning to dance energetically.

clue.text: Slim country and western singer with hired killer

parts.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with
a hitman is a hired assassin

explanation.surface: A thin cowboy crooner teams up with a contract killer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slim' looks like a description of the singer's build, but it is his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Slim Whitman was an American country and western singer famous for his yodelling falsetto.

clue.text: Gay song in the new musical

indicators.note: something new is remade, so the preceding letters are put into a fresh order

parts.note: the four words taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheerful number features in a brand-new stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything Goes is the 1934 Cole Porter stage musical, known for its title song.

clue.text: Tidy rapper adapted Beatles record

indicators.note: adapted means altered to fit, so the letters are reworked into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A neat hip-hop artist covers a track by the Beatles.
explanation.definitionFit: Day Tripper is a 1965 Beatles single, released as a double A-side with We Can Work It Out.

clue.text: Medley master's not arranged

indicators.note: arranged suggests letters set out in a new order, as music is arranged

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: The maestro has not yet scored the medley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' and 'Medley' pull towards music, but the medley is just a mixture here.
explanation.definitionFit: A medley is a varied mixture of things, which is exactly what an assortment is.

clue.text: Polish bandleader, Joe, after opening in Gdansk

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of the city name
Joe Loss was a popular British dance-band leader

explanation.surface: A Polish bandleader called Joe plays the opening night in Gdansk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' with its capital looks like the nationality, to go with Gdansk; it is the verb or noun polish. Joe Loss led one of Britain's best-known big bands from the 1930s on.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloss is a shine on a surface, the result of polishing, so it serves as a synonym of polish.

clue.text: Tenor spots headphones in bins

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for tenor
a rash is an outbreak of spots
cans is slang for headphones

explanation.surface: A tenor notices a pair of headphones thrown away in the rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spots' looks like a verb meaning sees; it is the skin complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Trash cans is the American term for rubbish bins.

clue.text: Verse form in short hymn I later changed about

indicators.note: changed about means shifted round, so the letters are mixed into a new order
a word made short has its last letter cut off

parts.note: taken as written, to be docked
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A short hymn I altered later on is now in a different verse form.
explanation.definitionFit: Tail rhyme is a stanza pattern in which rhyming lines are separated by short tail lines with their own rhyme.

clue.text: Rose, for example, can, cutting track

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates for example

indicators.note: something cutting into another goes inside it

parts.note: a lane is a narrow track
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: Rose, for instance, can cut a path through the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose, for example' looks like one phrase; Rose is the definition on its own. The can sits inside the track: LAN-TIN-E.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is the sweet briar, a wild rose with fragrant leaves.

clue.text: Opening bars of anthem — take it away!

definitions.text: Opening bars of anthem — take it away!

parts.note: surface reading: the first notes of a national song
setter's reading: the bandleader's cue to begin playing, which is exactly when the first bars come

explanation.surface: A conductor calls for the start of the anthem to be played.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take it away!' looks like a request to remove something, but it is the showbiz cue to start the music, so the whole clue describes the start of a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro is the introductory passage of a song, the opening bars before the main tune.

clue.text: Upset client, artist, a musician

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are tipped into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A disgruntled customer complains about the performer, a musician.
explanation.definitionFit: A clarinettist plays the clarinet, so is one kind of musician.

clue.text: Takes US singer "Stevie"

definitions.meaning: first meaning: steals, in British slang
second meaning: the surname of the Fleetwood Mac vocalist

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang to nick something is to steal it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevie Nicks is the American singer of Fleetwood Mac, and nicks is informal British for steals.

clue.text: Faith, for example, shown by a mother

parts.note: taken as written
a dam is the mother of an animal, especially a horse

explanation.surface: A mother demonstrates her religious faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faith' looks like belief; it is the surname of Adam Faith, a British pop singer of the late 1950s and 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Faith was an English pop singer and actor, so he is one example of a person called Adam.

clue.text: Old pop group docked in small Scottish port

indicators.note: docking cuts off a tail, so the last letter is removed

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a pop group is a band

explanation.surface: A veteran pop group's tour boat ties up in a little Scottish harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' looks like a ship mooring, which suits the port, but it means cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Oban is a small ferry port on the west coast of Scotland, gateway to the Hebrides.

clue.text: Composer, extremely diverse, occupied penning most original of songs

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of a word, its first and last letters

parts.note: first and last letters of the word

indicators.note: penning means writing down or enclosing, so one piece holds another

parts.note: busy means occupied

indicators.note: the most original part of a word is its very first letter

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A composer with very varied interests is kept busy writing the most original songs.
explanation.walkthrough: The busy piece holds the single letter from songs: BUS-S-Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude Debussy was the French composer of Clair de Lune and La Mer.

clue.text: Man, leader of choir, reportedly pleased

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of the word

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: pleased means glad, and the ending sounds the same spelt -IE

explanation.surface: A man who leads the choir is said to be delighted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader of choir' looks like a conductor; it gives a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Chappie is an informal, old-fashioned British word for a man or fellow, a diminutive of chap.

clue.text: Troupe of musicians, male, in street playing lyres

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for male

indicators.note: playing with letters means moving them about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
St is the abbreviation for street
taken as written

explanation.surface: Street musicians, including a man, are out playing their lyres.
explanation.definitionFit: Minstrelsy can mean a body of minstrels, a group of travelling singers and musicians.

clue.text: Part of a Gibson, say, about to be wrapped in pink paper

indicators.note: something wrapped in another sits inside it

parts.note: the Financial Times is printed on pink paper
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A Gibson guitar is about to be gift-wrapped in pink paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Financial Times, the British business daily, is famous for its salmon-pink pages; RE goes inside its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Frets are the raised metal strips across a guitar neck, and Gibson is a famous guitar maker.
